title: My First Solo Trip: Four Days in Mendoza
focus: Modals of advice and first conditional
paragraphs: Last October, Lautaro, a nineteen-year-old student from Córdoba, took his first solo trip: four days in Mendoza, a city near the Andes Mountains in Argentina. His parents were worried, but he was determined. Here is what he learnt, and what he would do differently next time.

Before he left, Lautaro made a plan. He wrote down the address of his hostel, the bus times and the phone numbers of two relatives. He sent this information to his mother and promised to message her every evening. 'If she knows where I am, she will worry less, and I will feel safer,' he says.

On the bus, he kept his documents in a small bag under his clothes, and he saved a photo of his ID card on his phone. He also put a little money in a different pocket, because he had read that you shouldn't keep all your cash in one place. 'I never showed my wallet in the street,' he adds. 'If people can't see it, they won't think about it.'

The best decision, however, was choosing a hostel with good reviews and a common kitchen. On the second night, he cooked pasta with two German travellers and a girl from Chile. The next day they rented bicycles together and visited a park and a small museum. 'If I stayed in a private hotel, I would probably spend the whole trip alone,' says Lautaro.

Not everything was perfect. He lost half a day because he missed a bus, and he felt homesick on the third night. But he says that the difficult moments taught him more than the easy ones. His advice for first-time solo travellers: plan the basics, trust your instincts, and say yes to new people, but always in public places. 'Travelling alone doesn't mean being lonely,' he says. 'It means learning to depend on yourself.'

title: Level Up: A School Esports Team
focus: Present perfect and connectors of contrast
paragraphs: At first, many teachers laughed when Thiago Alves, sixteen, asked for permission to start an esports team at his school in São Paulo. 'They thought it was just a way to play video games during lunch,' he says. Today the team has twelve members and its own classroom, and the same teachers come to watch their matches.

The rules are strict. The players practise only twice a week, for ninety minutes, and everyone must have passing grades in all subjects. If a student fails a test, he or she can't play until the grade improves. 'This rule was our coach's idea,' says Thiago. 'Ms Nakamura says that a good player is also a good student.'

Practice is not only about pressing buttons. The team studies videos of their matches, discusses mistakes and decides new strategies. They also have to communicate quickly and clearly, because a five-second delay can lose a game. Since many of the online players they face are foreign, the students have started using English in their chats, and their teacher says that their vocabulary has improved.

Last month the team won the regional school tournament, beating eleven other schools. Each player received a small trophy and a new headset. Critics say that gaming is a waste of time and that young people spend too many hours in front of screens. Thiago accepts that this can be a real problem.

'But a game is not different from any other hobby,' he answers. 'If you do it all day, it's bad. If you do it with limits and friends, it can teach you teamwork, discipline and respect.' The team's next goal is to enter a national competition. Before that, however, they have a more important challenge: the maths exam next Friday.

title: Four Hives on a School Roof
focus: Passive voice and defining relative clauses
paragraphs: On the roof of a school in Lyon, France, there are four white boxes and about a hundred thousand residents who never go to class. They are bees, and they are the pride of the school's science club.

The project started two years ago, when a beekeeper named Mr Dubois offered to teach the students. At first many of them were afraid of being stung. They wore white suits, hats with nets and thick gloves, and they were told to move slowly. 'Bees can feel when you are nervous,' says Malik, sixteen. 'If you are calm, they are calm.'

Every hive has one queen, who lays eggs, and thousands of worker bees, who do everything else. In spring and summer, the workers fly out of the hive to look for nectar in parks, gardens and balconies. They can travel several kilometres from the roof. When they return, the nectar is changed into honey inside the hive.

Last summer, the club collected sixty jars of honey. The honey was sold at the school fair, and the money was used to buy a microscope. Students also learnt that the honey of each season tastes different, because it depends on the flowers that the bees have visited. 'Our spring honey is light and sweet,' says Malik. 'The summer one is darker and stronger.'

The project has a serious purpose, too. Bees help plants to produce fruit by moving pollen from flower to flower, but in some regions their numbers are falling. The students have planted flowers on the roof and put a small bowl of water near the hives. 'We can't save the world with four boxes,' says Mr Dubois, 'but we can teach a new generation to care about nature.'

title: My Worst Day at the Café
paragraphs: I got my first job at sixteen, in a small café in Lima. The manager, Doña Carmen, gave me an apron, a notebook and one piece of advice: 'Smile, and everything else will be easier.' I smiled so much on my first day that my cheeks hurt by lunchtime.

My second day was the disaster. At eleven o'clock, a customer asked for a coffee with milk and a sandwich, and I brought a tea with lemon and a salad. 'There must be a mistake,' he said politely. I apologised and ran back to the kitchen, where I dropped a tray of glasses. The noise was so loud that everybody turned to look at me.

Then it got worse. A woman wanted to pay for her breakfast, which cost eighteen soles, and I gave her change for a fifty-sol note when she had given me a twenty. Luckily, my coworker Alonso noticed my mistake before she left. I wanted to hide in the fridge, but Doña Carmen was already walking towards me.

I was sure that she would fire me. Instead, she took me to the back of the café and gave me a glass of water. 'When I started working here twenty years ago,' she said, 'I once served salt instead of sugar to the mayor's wife. I cried for an hour. Nobody learns this job without mistakes. The important thing is to learn from them.'

She taught me a simple system: repeat the order to the customer before writing it, and count the change twice. I used it every day after that. Three months later, I had not made a single mistake in a week, and Doña Carmen gave me a small raise. I still smile at every customer, and I always tell new employees my story on their second day.

title: A Letter to the Editor: We Need a Skate Park
focus: Giving opinions and defending an argument
paragraphs: Dear Editor,

I am writing about the skate park that our neighbourhood in Cali has been waiting for during the last five years. Every afternoon, more than forty teenagers skate on the pavement outside the sports centre, because there is nowhere else to go. Last week, a security guard shouted at them and a neighbour called the police. Nobody was hurt, but the situation could be dangerous.

Some people say that skating is noisy and that skaters cause problems. I understand that opinion, but I disagree. A skate park would take young people off the streets, and it would give them a safe place where they could practise. If the skaters were in one place, the noise would not bother the neighbours.

Skating is also good for health. It is a sport that develops balance, courage and patience. Many of us don't enjoy football or basketball, and a skate park would offer another option. In addition, other cities in the region have built similar parks, and they have become popular meeting points for families, not just teenagers.

We have done our homework. We have found an empty lot, which belongs to the city, near the river path. In two weeks we collected 1,200 signatures from neighbours, shop owners and teachers. We are also willing to help with the design, and we could organise volunteers to keep the park clean.

I hope that the council will study our proposal seriously. We are not asking for anything luxurious, just a few ramps and a flat area. Young people need places where they can belong. Please give us a chance.
Yours faithfully,
Yesenia Mosquera
glossary: pertenecer, sentirse parte de un lugar

title: Through the Lens: Photographing the Galápagos
paragraphs: Gabriela Intriago, twenty-six, has photographed animals in the Galápagos Islands, in Ecuador, for four years. Her photos have appeared in magazines in several countries, but she says her career started with a very cheap camera. 'My father gave it to me when I was twelve,' she says. 'It cost forty dollars, and I took it everywhere.'

She explained that wildlife photography is mostly about waiting. 'You can sit for five hours in the same place, and sometimes nothing happens,' she said. 'Then, in thirty seconds, a blue-footed booby dives into the water and you have to be ready.' She added that patience is more important than expensive equipment.

Respect for the animals is the first rule. In the Galápagos, visitors must keep a safe distance and are not allowed to touch or feed any animal. Gabriela said that she once waited two hours for an iguana to move, and she never went closer. 'If the animal changes its behaviour because of you, the photo is not honest,' she explained.

She also uses her work to protect the islands. Last year she organised an exhibition in Guayaquil, and she told visitors about the problems that the islands face, such as plastic in the ocean. All the money from the sale of photographs, about three thousand dollars, went to a local conservation group.

When asked what advice she would give to young photographers, Gabriela said that they should start with what is near them. 'You don't need to travel to an island,' she said. 'Photograph the birds in your park, the insects in your garden, the dog in your street. Learn to see, and the camera will follow.' She smiled and added that her first photo was of a pigeon.

title: Teenage Guides of the Walled City
paragraphs: Every Saturday morning, a group of teenagers in orange T-shirts waits near the main gate of the old walled city in Cartagena. They aren't waiting for a bus. They are tour guides, and they have been trained by a local foundation to show visitors the history of their city in English.

The programme, which is free for students from public schools, lasts six months. Participants learn about the city's history, practise their English and study how to talk in front of a group. In the last month, each teenager must pass a final exam: a real tour of forty-five minutes with a teacher watching. Only those who pass are given an official badge.

Dilan Pérez, sixteen, was one of the first students. 'I used to be very shy,' he says. 'Now I can talk to thirty strangers without feeling nervous.' His favourite story is about the thick stone walls, which were built hundreds of years ago to protect the city from pirates. He tells it with a deep, dramatic voice and always makes the visitors laugh.

The guides don't get a salary, but visitors usually give tips, and the money is divided among the group. With his share, Dilan has paid for his English course and bought a bicycle. Another guide, Yasmín Ortiz, says that she has saved enough to enter a tourism course next year. 'Before this programme,' she says, 'I didn't know that I could have a career in my own city.'

Not everyone is enthusiastic. Some professional guides worry that teenagers will take their customers, and a few tourists prefer to hire an experienced person. The foundation answers that the teenagers only work on Saturdays and offer a different, more personal experience. 'We are not competing,' says the director. 'We are preparing future colleagues.'

title: The Day the Wi-Fi Died
paragraphs: It was nine o'clock on Saturday morning in Santo Domingo when the Wi-Fi stopped working. My sister Ariana was watching a video, my dad was joining a work call, my mum was following a recipe online, and I was playing a game with my friends. Suddenly, everything stopped, and four faces looked at the router in horror.

'It's just a small problem,' said Dad. He unplugged the router, counted to ten and plugged it in again. Nothing happened. He called the company, but their phone line was busy for forty minutes. When somebody finally answered, the technician said that a cable had been damaged in the storm and that it wouldn't be repaired until Monday.

Two days without internet! Ariana started to cry in a dramatic way, and I lay on the sofa like a dead fish. Mum decided that she didn't need a recipe because she had cooked arroz con pollo a hundred times. Dad said that he would go to a café to work, but all the cafés in the neighbourhood were full of people with the same idea.

By lunchtime, we were bored. Then Ariana found an old box of board games behind the wardrobe. We played dominoes, which is very popular in our country, for three hours. Dad, who claimed that he had never lost a game, lost four times in a row, and Mum laughed so much that she burned the rice.

That evening, we sat on the balcony and talked. I learnt that Dad had played baseball when he was young, and that Mum had once wanted to be a singer. We had lived in the same house for years, but we had never had such a long conversation. On Monday morning, the internet came back. For about ten minutes, we all stared at our screens. Then Ariana said, 'Does anyone want to play dominoes tonight?'

title: How to Make a Podcast with Your Class
paragraphs: Making a podcast is easier than you think, and you don't need expensive equipment. Last term, my class of fifteen-year-olds made a six-episode series about local history, and we learnt a lot in the process. Here is the method that worked for us.

First, choose a topic that everyone likes. Hold a vote, but make sure that the topic is specific. 'Music' is too general, but 'the history of music in our town' is perfect. Then decide on a format: an interview, a discussion between friends or a story. Each episode should last between five and ten minutes.

Second, prepare a short plan, not a full script. Write the main ideas on a card and practise saying them in your own words. If you read a text, your voice will sound stiff. For an interview, write five open questions in advance, and don't forget to ask permission from the person that you are going to record.

Third, find a quiet place. We recorded in a small storeroom full of coats, because the clothes absorbed the echo. Put your phone on a soft surface and speak about ten centimetres from the microphone. Before you start, do a thirty-second test. If you hear traffic, a fan or a noisy corridor, change the place. It is much harder to fix bad sound later.

Finally, edit and share. Use a free program to cut the mistakes, and add some music at the start. Ask your teacher where you can publish the episodes safely. Never include full names, addresses or phone numbers. When you have finished, listen to the audience's comments and use them to improve the next episode. Our last episode had two hundred listeners, and we were so proud!

title: The Baker Who Starts at Midnight
focus: Present simple, present continuous and present perfect
paragraphs: While most people in Córdoba are sleeping, Ramiro Bustos is already working. His day begins at midnight, when he opens the door of the bakery where he has worked for eleven years. The streets are empty, and the only sound is the radio in the corner of the kitchen.

First, he lights the oven, which takes about an hour to get hot. Meanwhile, he prepares the dough for bread and for facturas, the sweet pastries that Argentinians love with their morning coffee. His hands move quickly because he has done this thousands of times. 'I don't measure everything,' he says. 'After eleven years, I can feel when the dough is right.'

By four o'clock, the first loaves are ready, and the shop smells wonderful. The first customers are usually taxi drivers, nurses and workers who are finishing the night shift. They buy warm bread and chat for a few minutes. 'They are tired, but they always smile,' says Ramiro. 'Maybe it's because of the smell.'

Of course, the job has disadvantages. Ramiro sleeps from ten in the morning until three in the afternoon, so he misses many family lunches and his friends' parties. 'My daughter is seven,' he says, 'and she is asleep when I leave and at school when I come home. That is the hardest part.' To spend time together, he makes dinner for her every evening at seven, and they talk until bedtime.

Ramiro is not planning to change jobs. He says that being a baker means giving people a good start to their day. His dream is to open a small school for young bakers in his neighbourhood, because many of them can't find a job. 'It's tiring work,' he admits, 'but when I see someone eating my bread, I'm the happiest person in the city.'
